blocks.directed: [long pause] Śiva Sūtras 3.2
[slowly] ज्ञानं बन्धः
Jñānaṃ bandhaḥ.
Knowledge is bondage.

blocks.text: Knowledge Is Bondage. Yes, Again. Apparently You Didn’t Get It the First Time.
blocks.directed: Knowledge Is Bondage. Yes, Again. Apparently You Didn’t Get It the First Time.
RIGHT.
WE’VE SEEN THIS ONE.

blocks.text: It’s literally the second sūtra of the first book.
blocks.directed: It’s literally the second sūtra of the first book.

blocks.text: Vasugupta has copied and pasted himself.
blocks.directed: Vasugupta has copied and pasted himself.

blocks.text: The man’s producing sacred scripture and apparently can’t be bothered writing a new sentence.
blocks.directed: The man’s producing sacred scripture and apparently can’t be bothered writing a new sentence.

blocks.text: But the repetition is entirely deliberate.
blocks.directed: But the repetition is entirely deliberate.

blocks.text: Because the same statement is now being explained from the standpoint of the limited individual.
blocks.directed: Because the same statement is now being explained from the standpoint of the limited individual.

blocks.text: In Book I, knowledge as bondage was connected with the fundamental contraction of universal consciousness.
blocks.directed: In Book I, knowledge as bondage was connected with the fundamental contraction of universal consciousness.

blocks.text: Here, Kṣemarāja gets much more specific.
blocks.directed: Here, Kṣemarāja gets much more specific.

blocks.text: He’s talking about the ordinary mental cognitions associated with:
blocks.directed: [short pause] He’s talking about the ordinary mental cognitions associated with:
Pleasure.
Pain.
Delusion.
Judgement.
Appropriation.
The perception of difference.

blocks.text: And the experience of being an individual subject moving through a world of external objects.
blocks.directed: And the experience of being an individual subject moving through a world of external objects.

blocks.text: Now imagine you’re having a perfectly pleasant afternoon.
blocks.directed: Now imagine you’re having a perfectly pleasant afternoon.
You see something beautiful.
[short pause] The mind responds:
[short pause] “I like this.”
[short pause] Then:
[short pause] “I want this.”
[short pause] Then:
[short pause] “I need to keep this.”
[short pause] Then:
[short pause] “What happens if I lose this?”
[short pause] Then:

blocks.text: “Why does that bastard have a better one?”
blocks.directed: [short pause] “Why does that bastard have a better one?”

blocks.text: And within approximately seventeen seconds, an innocent pleasant perception has developed into a complete metaphysical hostage situation.
blocks.directed: And within approximately seventeen seconds, an innocent pleasant perception has developed into a complete metaphysical hostage situation.

blocks.text: Now, Kṣemarāja isn’t suggesting that pleasure is intrinsically sinful.
blocks.directed: Now, Kṣemarāja isn’t suggesting that pleasure is intrinsically sinful.

blocks.text: Nor that distinguishing objects is itself an ethical failure.
blocks.directed: Nor that distinguishing objects is itself an ethical failure.

blocks.text: The issue is that differentiated knowledge becomes entangled with limited identity.
blocks.directed: The issue is that differentiated knowledge becomes entangled with limited identity.

blocks.text: The individual knows through an apparatus already structured by the conditions of limitation.
blocks.directed: The individual knows through an apparatus already structured by the conditions of limitation.

blocks.text: And so every act of knowing can reinforce the apparent division between the finite knower and the independent known.
blocks.directed: And so every act of knowing can reinforce the apparent division between the finite knower and the independent known.
[short pause] The limited person begins from:
[short pause] “I am here.”
[short pause] “The world is over there.”
[short pause] “I must obtain what completes me.”
[short pause] “I must resist what threatens me.”

blocks.text: And all these experiences produce further involvement in saṃsāra.
blocks.directed: And all these experiences produce further involvement in saṃsāra.

blocks.text: Kṣemarāja connects this process with puryaṣṭaka.
blocks.directed: Kṣemarāja connects this process with puryaṣṭaka.
The eightfold subtle constitution.

blocks.text: Traditionally comprising the intellect, ego, ordinary mind and five subtle sensory elements.
blocks.directed: Traditionally comprising the intellect, ego, ordinary mind and five subtle sensory elements.

blocks.text: This subtle constitution, together with karmic tendencies, is implicated in transmigration.
blocks.directed: This subtle constitution, together with karmic tendencies, is implicated in transmigration.

blocks.text: He draws on the Spandakārikā to describe the bound individual experiencing pleasure, pain and successive forms of existence through the activities of the subtle body. Sanskrit & Trika Shaivism.
blocks.directed: He draws on the Spandakārikā to describe the bound individual experiencing pleasure, pain and successive forms of existence through the activities of the subtle body. Sanskrit & Trika Shaivism.

blocks.text: Now here’s what makes this so philosophically interesting.
blocks.directed: Now here’s what makes this so philosophically interesting.

blocks.text: The actual problem isn’t that the mind knows something.
blocks.directed: The actual problem isn’t that the mind knows something.

blocks.text: Because from the standpoint of Trika, even the act of limited knowing is a manifestation of consciousness.
blocks.directed: Because from the standpoint of Trika, even the act of limited knowing is a manifestation of consciousness.

blocks.text: The problem is the failure to recognise the conscious reality of the knower and the known.
blocks.directed: The problem is the failure to recognise the conscious reality of the knower and the known.

blocks.text: Suppose I look at a flower.
blocks.directed: Suppose I look at a flower.
There’s a cognition.
[short pause] “Flower.”
There’s a perceiver.
[short pause] “Me.”
There’s a perceived object.
[short pause] “That flower.”

blocks.text: Ordinary experience organises those into a relation of difference.
blocks.directed: Ordinary experience organises those into a relation of difference.

blocks.text: Now, at the conventional level, that’s perfectly functional.
blocks.directed: Now, at the conventional level, that’s perfectly functional.

blocks.text: You shouldn’t try to water yourself because you’ve decided the distinction between you and the flower is ultimately nondual.
blocks.directed: You shouldn’t try to water yourself because you’ve decided the distinction between you and the flower is ultimately nondual.
The flower still needs water.
You probably need breakfast.

blocks.text: But at the metaphysical level, the Trika claim is that the perceiver, perception and perceived object are not ultimately independent of the one self-revealing consciousness.
blocks.directed: But at the metaphysical level, the Trika claim is that the perceiver, perception and perceived object are not ultimately independent of the one self-revealing consciousness.

blocks.text: And without that recognition, the subject mistakes their finite cognitive standpoint for their complete nature.
blocks.directed: And without that recognition, the subject mistakes their finite cognitive standpoint for their complete nature.

blocks.text: So the same world can be experienced through two fundamentally different orientations.
blocks.directed: So the same world can be experienced through two fundamentally different orientations.
One: limited knowledge reinforcing separation.

blocks.text: The other: differentiated cognition recognised as the manifestation of consciousness.
blocks.directed: The other: differentiated cognition recognised as the manifestation of consciousness.

blocks.text: And Vasugupta’s point is that the former constitutes bondage.
blocks.directed: And Vasugupta’s point is that the former constitutes bondage.

blocks.text: Which brings us to a very uncomfortable question.
blocks.directed: Which brings us to a very uncomfortable question.

blocks.text: Why does consciousness fail to recognise its own nature?
blocks.directed: Why does consciousness fail to recognise its own nature?
Enter Māyā.
Again.
She’s back.
And she’s brought paperwork.
